original_summary: Modern Art is a 3-5 player auction game. Players take turns auctioning painting cards by five artists using five different auction formats. At the end of each of four seasons, the artists played most often gain value, and owned paintings of those artists pay out. The player with the most money wins.

review.evidence: Simple policies lose. A player who never bids gets only paintings nobody else wants and falls behind. A player who always bids high overpays for artists that may never score. The auctioneer seat rotates, so no seat has a built-in edge, and each auction choice changes which artists score.

Valuing a painting means predicting which artists will finish in the top three. That depends on rivals' hands and incentives, so good valuation and timing reliably beat naive bidding. The deal adds variance, but over four seasons skill dominates.

Strong players keep improving: they manipulate rankings, choose which cards to sell, end seasons early and read rivals' money. A weak player can still score by buying cheap paintings of leading artists.
Hands and money are hidden. Players must infer which artists rivals will push and how much they can afford, and plan across seasons because artist values accumulate.
Payouts, prices and the final money comparison are pure arithmetic.

Five auction formats, five artists, large hands, open ascending bidding (close to real time) and a value board make the game far too long and rule-heavy for the step and choice limits. It needs heavy compression.

problems: The original is too large for the platform: five auction types, five artists, large hands and four long seasons exceed the step and choice limits, and open ascending bidding is close to real time.
In the previous variation, the rules after scoring (payout, reset, announce) had no explicit condition. A flat step list read literally would wipe all paintings every round, which destroys the game.

The previous variation did not say whether talk exists. The game has three players with real conflict (auctioneer wants high prices, bidders want low prices, only one player can win), so the omission leaves the design incomplete.
The previous variation claimed money was private while announcing every bid, price and payout. Every balance could be computed exactly, so the claim was misleading about what is hidden.
The auction steps (bid, winner, settle) in the previous variation also relied on prose to be skipped when the played card ends the season, rather than on an explicit tracked condition.

changes.what: Compress the game to 3 players, 3 artists, 7-card hands with symmetric compositions (4/2/1), one sealed-bid auction format, seasons ending on the 3rd card of an artist, and 18 rounds.
changes.why: This keeps auctions, season rankings and accumulating artist values within 15 steps per round and 3 choice steps per round.
changes.fixes: The original is too large for the platform: five auction types, five artists, large hands and four long seasons exceed the step and choice limits, and open ascending bidding is close to real time.

changes.what: Add a single table flag, season_over. It is cleared at the start of every round, set to 1 by a season-ending card, and set to 1 in round 18. Scoring, payout, reset and season announcement each carry the explicit condition 'only if season_over = 1'. Rotation, the round counter and the end check are stated to run every round.
changes.why: A literal flat-list engine then can never wipe paintings in a round where no season ended.
changes.fixes: In the previous variation, the rules after scoring (payout, reset, announce) had no explicit condition. A flat step list read literally would wipe all paintings every round, which destroys the game.

changes.what: Give talk, bid, winner and settle the explicit condition 'only if season_over = 0' at that point, before the round-18 flag is set.
changes.why: A season-ending card is then never auctioned, through a tracked number rather than prose.
changes.fixes: The previous variation's auction steps (bid, winner, settle) relied on prose to be skipped when the played card ends the season, rather than on an explicit tracked condition.

changes.what: Add one simultaneous talk step each auctioned round, after the card is revealed and before bids. Every player writes one short message without seeing the others; all messages are then shown; then everyone bids. Talk is non-binding.
changes.why: The game passes both talk tests. Players disagree: the auctioneer wants high bids, bidders want low prices, and only one player can win. Talk gives bluffing about hand composition and interest, and offers non-binding low-bid pacts that a rival can betray to grab the painting cheaply. Talk is simultaneous so that no one simply copies an earlier speaker.
changes.fixes: The previous variation did not say whether talk exists. The game has three players with real conflict (auctioneer wants high prices, bidders want low prices, only one player can win), so the omission leaves the design incomplete.

changes.what: Declare money public. Each seat's hand composition remains the single hidden element.
changes.why: The stated hidden information then matches what players can actually compute. The real inference is about who holds which composition, and therefore which artist each rival will push or end.
changes.fixes: The previous variation claimed money was private while announcing every bid, price and payout. Every balance could be computed exactly, so the claim was misleading about what is hidden.

keeps: Players take turns as auctioneer and sell a card from their own hand.
A seller who buys their own painting pays the bank; otherwise the buyer pays the seller.
A season ends when a set number of cards of one artist has been played, and the ending card is not sold.
Artists are ranked by cards played in the season. Top artists gain value that accumulates across seasons, and owned paintings pay the artist's cumulative value.
Paintings are discarded after each season.
Most money at the end wins.

recommendation.reason: The core of Modern Art (valuing paintings by predicting artist rankings, deciding which cards to sell and when to end a season) survives compression to three artists and one sealed-bid format, within the limits.

variation.name: Modern Art: Sealed Gallery
variation.summary: Three players each hold a hidden hand of seven paintings across three artists, in compositions 4/2/1 that are worth the same in total. They take turns as auctioneer, offering one painting per round to a simultaneous sealed-bid auction preceded by one round of simultaneous talk. The third painting of an artist in a season ends the season and is not sold. Artists ranked first and second gain value that accumulates over the game, owned paintings pay out, and after 18 rounds the richest player wins.
variation.rules:
R1 SETUP (once, before round 1). There are three players, seats 1, 2 and 3, and three artists: Red, Blue and Green.
- Every player starts with money 60 and with owned_red, owned_blue and owned_green all 0.
- Each artist starts with season count 0 and value 0.
- The auctioneer is seat 1. The round counter is 0. The flag season_over is 0.
- Money is public: every bid, price and payout is announced, and anyone may track every balance. Each player's hand is private.

R2 DEAL (once, before round 1). The game rolls one six-sided die (deal_roll, 1 to 6).
- The three compositions are:
  - A: Red 4, Blue 2, Green 1.
  - B: Red 1, Blue 4, Green 2.
  - C: Red 2, Blue 1, Green 4.
- Seats 1, 2 and 3 receive compositions by roll:
  - Roll 1: A, B, C.
  - Roll 2: A, C, B.
  - Roll 3: B, A, C.
  - Roll 4: B, C, A.
  - Roll 5: C, A, B.
  - Roll 6: C, B, A.
- Exactly one case applies. It SETS each seat's hand_red, hand_blue and hand_green to the listed numbers.
- Each player sees only their own hand. Each player knows the other two seats hold the other two compositions, but not which seat holds which.

Each round runs R3 to R16 in order.

R3 START (every round). The round counter rises by 1. season_over is set to 0.

R4 PLAY (every round). The auctioneer chooses one artist X for which their own hand count is above 0. Only those artists are options.

R5 UPDATE (every round).
- The auctioneer's hand_X falls by 1.
- season_X rises by 1.
- current_artist is set to X and announced to all.

R6 SEASON-ENDING CARD (every round). If season_X is now 3, season_over is set to 1, the card is discarded unsold, and this is announced. Otherwise season_over stays 0.

R7 TALK (only if season_over = 0). Every player, including the auctioneer, writes one short message at the same time without seeing the others. All three messages are then shown to everyone, labelled by seat. Messages are free text and bind no one.

R8 BID (only if season_over = 0). All three players, including the auctioneer, bid at the same moment.
- Each bids a whole number from 0 up to their own current money.
- Bids are hidden until all are in, then all three are announced.

R9 WINNER (only if season_over = 0).
- The highest bid wins, and the price is the winning bid.
- If the highest bid is 0, the auctioneer takes the painting at price 0.
- Ties at a positive bid go to the tied seat that comes first in this order: the seat after the auctioneer, then the next seat, with the auctioneer last. (Auctioneer 1: order 2, 3, 1. Auctioneer 2: order 3, 1, 2. Auctioneer 3: order 1, 2, 3.)

R10 SETTLE (only if season_over = 0).
- If the winner is not the auctioneer, the winner's money falls by the price and the auctioneer's money rises by the price.
- If the winner is the auctioneer, the auctioneer's money falls by the price, which goes to the bank.
- The winner's owned_X rises by 1.
- The winner and price are announced.

R11 FINAL-ROUND FLAG (every round). If the round counter is 18, season_over is set to 1.

R12 SEASON SCORING (only if season_over = 1). Only artists with season count at least 1 can score.
- If one artist has the strictly highest season count, its value rises by 6. Then, if one of the other two artists has a strictly higher season count than the third and at least 1, that artist's value rises by 3.
- If two or three artists tie for the highest season count (at least 1), each of them gains value +3, and no other artist scores.

R13 PAYOUT (only if season_over = 1). For each artist that scored in R12 this round, every player's money rises by (their owned count of that artist) × (that artist's new cumulative value). Artists that did not score pay nothing, but keep their value.

R14 RESET (only if season_over = 1).
- Every player's owned_red, owned_blue and owned_green become 0 (paintings are discarded).
- Every artist's season count becomes 0.
- Values are kept.

R15 ANNOUNCE (only if season_over = 1). The scoring artists, their new values, each player's payout and each player's money are announced.

R16 ROTATE AND END (every round).
- The auctioneer passes to the next seat (1 to 2, 2 to 3, 3 to 1).
- If the round counter is 18, the game ends. Otherwise the next round begins at R3.
- Each seat is auctioneer exactly 6 times and plays 6 of its 7 cards, so the R4 options are never empty.
variation.objective: After round 18, including the final season's scoring and payout, the player with the strictly highest money wins. If two or three players tie for the highest money, the game is a draw.
variation.expected_effect:
Bids now hinge on predicting which artists will rank first and second this season and how values will accumulate. That prediction depends on inferring which composition each rival holds from what they auction, how they bid and what they say. Auctioneers choose which card to sell, and whether to end a season by playing an artist's third card, to strand rivals' paintings or cash in their own. Because compositions are symmetric (each seat holds one 4, one 2 and one 1), the deal changes what to do, not who is ahead.

Talk passes both tests. The players disagree: the auctioneer wants high bids, each bidder wants the painting cheap, and only one player can win. Players can bluff about their composition to steer rivals toward or away from an artist, or propose that both bidders bid low against the auctioneer. Such a pact is non-binding: a player who follows it by bidding 0 loses the painting to a partner who defects with a small bid, and with it the payout that may decide the game. A player who believes a bluff about which artist will lead overpays for paintings that score nothing.

Simple policies lose. Always bidding 0 cedes every contested painting. Always bidding all your money bankrupts you on non-scoring artists. Always playing your largest artist lets rivals predict and exploit your season endings. The fixed-length, highest-total rule is appropriate here because this is a competitive auction, not a cooperation game, so there is no trust for endgame unravelling to destroy.

balanced.evidence:
Single-painting payoff, value v (owned count times cumulative value at scoring) and price p. (a) Non-auctioneer buys: buyer v-p, auctioneer +p, third player 0. (b) Auctioneer buys: auctioneer v-p (paid to the bank), others 0. (c) All bid 0: auctioneer v, others 0.

Relative effect of a non-auctioneer purchase: buyer gains v-2p against the auctioneer and v-p against the third player. Sensible bids therefore sit around v/2 to v, not at a corner.

Typical values. In the first season the leader scores 6 and the runner-up 3; later seasons stack to 9, 12, 15 or 18. With 18 cards a season lasts 3 to 7 cards, so there are about 3 to 5 seasons, and most paintings are worth 3 to 12 against starting money of 60.

Thoughtless policies, judged by the winner rule:
(1) Always bid 0 (Z). Z never pays and earns only as auctioneer. When sensible A auctions, sensible B can win with bid 1 above A's shading bid. Example: v=6, A bids 3, B bids 4 gives B +2, A +4, Z 0. Over about 10 auctions not run by Z, Z forgoes both surplus and revenue it cannot recoup in its own 6 auctions (at most about v each, and only if A and B compete). Z falls behind and loses, though not by a fixed amount.
(2) Always bid all money. It wins round 1 or 2 at a price of 60, handing the auctioneer +60 for a painting worth at most 6 to 9. It is then broke and loses every time.
(3) Always bid 1. It wins only when the others bid 0 and loses to any sensible bidder.
(4) Always play the first option (Red if held). This only shapes season counts. It is exploitable by players who read the announced plays and bid on Red, and it does not guarantee a win.
No bid is strictly dominant, because first-price sealed bids against two rivals make the best bid depend on their bids.

Seats. The three compositions are rotations of (4,2,1), so the deal is symmetric across artists. Each seat is auctioneer 6 times. The positive-tie order rotates with the auctioneer. The card that ends a season earns its auctioneer nothing, but every seat faces that risk.
Seat 3 auctions round 18, the forced final scoring, but the value of that painting is common knowledge to all three bidders, so the edge is small.
All three players can realistically win.

playable.evidence:
(1) R10 to R13 are written as if they run only when a season scores, but only R10 states the condition. R12 RESET ('Every player's owned... become 0') has no 'only if scoring happened' clause. An engine with a flat step list and a model reading it literally may wipe paintings every round, which destroys the game. R11 and R13 have the same problem, while R14 must run every round. Each of R11, R12 and R13 needs an explicit when-condition.
(2) Three-player talk is not addressed at all. The players disagree: the auctioneer wants high bids and the bidders want low prices. Simultaneous talk before the bid could let two bidders try a non-binding pact to bid low against the auctioneer, or let them bluff interest. The design must state whether talk exists, and if it does, that it is simultaneous.
(3) 'Money is private' is cosmetic. Every bid, price and payout is announced, so every balance can be computed exactly. This is harmless but misleading about what is hidden.
(4) Limits: steps 15 (limit 20), choice steps 2 (limit 4), rounds 18 (limit 40), random draws 1 at setup (limit 1 per round), hidden elements 2 (limit 3). Attributes: per player there are money, hand x3 and owned x3 (7); the table has season x3, value x3, current_artist, auctioneer and deal_roll (9). That is 16 attribute types, within the stated 20.
(5) The game is finite and all scoring is arithmetic. No board, clock or judge is needed.
(6) Hands cannot run out, since each seat plays 6 of 7 cards. R3 options are always non-empty.

required_changes: Add an explicit condition to R11, R12 and R13: 'Only if scoring happened this round (R10).' State that R14 (rotate) and the round counter run every round.

Decide talk explicitly. Either add a simultaneous free-text talk step after R5 and before R7 bids (all write, all are shown, then all bid), justified by the auctioneer-versus-bidders conflict. Or state that there is no talk and why, for example that sealed-bid reasoning is the intended test.
Either drop the claim that money is private or stop announcing every price and payout, so that the stated hidden information matches what players can actually compute.

balanced.evidence:
PAINTING VALUES. Season scoring: the top artist gets +6 to its cumulative value and the clear second gets +3. Each painting owned pays the artist's NEW cumulative value. Season 1 paintings are therefore worth 6 (top), 3 (second) or 0. If the same artist tops again, it pays 12, then 18, and so on. The artist whose third card ends the season always has count 3. The other two have at most 2, so that artist always takes +6, and the R12 tie branch can only occur at the forced round-18 end. Supply: 18 cards are played. A season ends after 3 to 7 cards (the seventh is forced, since 2+2+2 is the maximum before a third card), so there are about 3 to 5 seasons. Late paintings (12 to 24) are large against the starting money of 60, so the stakes grow and early play is not irrelevant.

TRANSFER TABLE for one painting of value v sold at price p (relative money change):
| Winner | Buyer | Auctioneer | Third |
|---|---|---|---|
| Non-auctioneer | v-p | +p | 0 |
| Auctioneer | v-p (paid to bank) | same | 0 |
| Nobody bids (all 0) | auctioneer +v | - | 0 |
Under the winner rule, a buyer gains v-2p against the seller and v-p against the third player. Sensible bids therefore sit between about v/2 and v, and that valuation is uncertain because the season ranking is not yet known. There is real tension and no strictly better bid.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES under the winner rule:
(a) Always bid 0. This player never gains purchase surplus and only collects the prices other players pay for its roughly 5 sold cards. A sensible opponent earns sale revenue plus positive v-p on purchases, so the bid-0 player can and usually does lose. If everyone else bids 0, bidding 1 on any painting worth 3 or more beats it. Fails to dominate.
(b) Always bid all money. On round 1 this pays up to 60 for a painting worth at most 6, which is a near-certain loss.
(c) Always bid a fixed small amount, such as 1. Any opponent bidding 2 or more on valuable cards takes them, so it loses.
(d) Always play the first legal artist (Red first). This is predictable, so opponents can time season endings and bid on the artist that will top. It loses to sensible play.
(e) Random bids lose to valuation-based bids.
No policy never loses, and no option is strictly better whatever the opponents do.

SEAT EDGES. The tie-break (seat after the auctioneer first, auctioneer last) rotates. Over 18 rounds each seat is auctioneer 6 times, first in tie order 6 times and second 6 times, so it is symmetric. The compositions A, B and C are cyclic relabelings of the same 4/2/1 hand, and the artists start equal. The only asymmetry is that seat 1 opens each season cycle, and that is minor. All three seats can realistically win, and no labelled payoff ordering is misdescribed.

Minor note: in a three-player game, kingmaking is possible through who you sell to, but it is not degenerate.

playable.evidence:
COMPLETENESS. The rules cover every situation:
- Deal: six roll cases, exactly one applies.
- Season end: R6 discards the third card unsold, and R7 to R10 are skipped.
- Forced final season: R11 at round 18 sets the end flag; if R6 already set it, the season still scores only once.
- Scoring: R12 handles the strict top, the strict second (which must have count at least 1) and the tie case.
- Payout: owned count times new cumulative value; non-scoring artists keep their value.
- Reset: R14.
- Bidding: whole numbers from 0 to current money; an all-zero round gives the painting to the auctioneer free; ties at a positive bid follow an explicit order; payment goes to the auctioneer or, if the auctioneer wins, to the bank.
- Legal plays: R16's claim holds, since each seat plays 6 of 7 cards in its 6 turns, so the R4 options are never empty.
- Winner: highest money after round 18, with an explicit draw rule.

FINITE AND ARITHMETIC. The game lasts exactly 18 rounds and is decided by arithmetic on tracked numbers.

LIMITS.
- About 14 steps per round, within the limit of 20.
- Choice steps: play, talk and bid, so 3, within the limit of 4.
- Attributes: about 19, within 20. Per player: money, 3 owned and 3 hand counts. Global: 3 season counts, 3 values, auctioneer, round, season_over, current_artist, deal_roll and winner/price.
- Hidden elements: 1 (hands).
- Random draws: 1, made once in total.
- Rounds: 18.
The deal is a conditional set, the bid is a simultaneous poll and the hands are hidden, all of which are supported. The game needs no board, clock, trading or binding agreements.

TALK. Talk is simultaneous (all write, all are shown, then all bid), which suits a three-player game. It sits where interests genuinely conflict. Each player wants a different artist to top, because each holds a different 4-card artist. Each wants to buy cheaply and sell dearly, and each may seek a two-against-one deal on which artist to push. Following a proposal can cost the follower, so talk is not mere copying.

LATE ROUNDS. Late rounds remain contested auctions with valuation questions. There is no 'safe option' that wins late rounds.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
CHANCE. The only random element is one die roll that assigns three relabeled-identical compositions to seats. Since the artists are symmetric at the start, the roll only fixes which artist each seat is long in and the cyclic or anticyclic orientation against seat order. Its effect on the result is small, an estimated 10 to 15%.

EQUAL GOOD PLAY. If all three players play well, the result is decided by:
- seat position in the season-ending sequence;
- control of the third card of each artist;
- auction pricing.
It is not decided by the die alone. A good player can overcome a weaker orientation.

WHAT CAN BE INFERRED.
- Hands: you know your own composition, so each opponent is one of two. Their plays, with counts 4, 2 or 1, quickly identify them. That tells you who can still end a given artist's season and who is short.
- Bids: revealed bids show what each opponent expects to score.

WAYS TO ACT ON IT.
- Choosing which artist to auction, which steers the ranking and season timing. Playing or forcing a third card ends the season before rivals' paintings of another artist pay.
- Bidding between v/2 and v according to the expected ranking.
- Using talk to form or break coalitions.

A reasoning player clearly beats a policy player.
